# Spectral analysis (`spectroscopy`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs spectrum_colour; helped by telescope, achromatic_lens
- Core idea: Each chemical element, heated in a flame or a spark, gives light of its own fixed colours, which a prism behind a narrow slit shows as sharp bright lines: sodium (common salt) a close yellow doublet, potassium violet, lithium red, copper green. A trace too small to weigh can be identified this way. The Sun's spectrum is crossed by hundreds of dark lines at the same places, because the cooler gas above its surface absorbs those colours; so we can tell what the Sun and stars are made of, and new elements have been found by unknown lines.
- Pitfalls:
  - Without a narrow slit the lines smear into a band
  - Sodium contamination makes almost every flame yellow
  - Judging by flame colour alone without the prism
- History: europe: 1752 Melvill notes the yellow line of salt in flames; 1802 Wollaston and 1814 Fraunhofer map dark lines in sunlight; 1859–1861 Kirchhoff and Bunsen establish spectral analysis, discovering caesium in 1860 and rubidium in 1861; 1868 helium seen in the Sun before it is found on Earth (1895)
- Read:
  - Gustav Kirchhoff & Robert Bunsen, Chemische Analyse durch Spectralbeobachtungen, Annalen der Physik 110 (1860)
  - John B. Hearnshaw, The Analysis of Starlight (1986)
